Yes — dplyr CRAN downloads are still growing on a year-over-year basis, though the last couple of months show a dip from a spring peak.

**Year-over-year (CRAN daily downloads, from `velocirepo/data/metrics/cran/dplyr/`):**

| Period | Avg daily downloads |
|---|---|
| 2022 | ~61,300 |
| 2023 | ~54,100 |
| 2024 | ~49,600 |
| 2025 | ~54,500 |
| Jan–Jul 2025 | ~50,600 |
| Jan–Jul 2026 (through 7/27, latest data available) | ~60,900 |

So compared to the same Jan–Jul window last year, downloads are up about **+20%**. The multi-year picture is a rise from 2019 through 2022, a dip in 2023–2024, and renewed growth through 2025 into 2026.

**But the most recent months show a slowdown, not growth:**

| Month (2026) | Avg daily downloads |
|---|---|
| Jan | ~54,800 |
| Feb | ~58,600 |
| Mar | ~63,400 |
| Apr | ~70,100 (peak) |
| May | ~61,400 |
| Jun | ~62,200 |
| Jul (partial, through 7/27) | ~55,100 |

So the trend within 2026 peaked in April and has been declining since — July is back down near January's level. I don't have August data yet (the most recent daily file is 2026-07-27), so I can't say whether this is a temporary dip or a genuine reversal of the longer-term growth trend.

**Bottom line:** Year-over-year, dplyr downloads are still up meaningfully vs. 2025. But the last three months (May–Jul 2026) show a decline from the April peak, so "still growing" depends on the time window — the long-term trend is positive, but the most recent short-term trend is downward. This is CRAN download data only (no PyPI, since dplyr is R-only); I don't have data past July 27, 2026.

Short answer: **it's real for some packages, but not universal — and the biggest one, Shiny, actually goes the other way.**

Using CRAN and PyPI daily-download data in this repo (latest data runs through 2026‑07‑27/28, so "recent" below = the 30 days ending then), here's how the Python vs. R releases of the same tools compare:

| Product pair | Python (30d downloads) | R (30d downloads) | Ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| Shiny (`shiny-python` vs `shiny-r`) | 269,169 | **808,389** | R is ~3x Python |
| Tables (`great-tables` vs `gt`) | **632,755** | 117,398 | Python is ~5.4x R |
| GenAI (`chatlas` vs `ellmer`) | **117,047** | 21,710 | Python is ~5.4x R |
| pointblank (`pointblank-python` vs `pointblank-r`) | **33,068** | 1,937 | Python is ~17x R |
| Plotting (`plotnine` vs `ggplot2`) | **3,290,323** | 2,142,748 | Python is ~1.5x R (both huge) |
| orbital (`orbital-python` vs `orbital-r`) | **3,891** | 386 | Python is ~10x R (both tiny) |
| querychat (same name both places) | **3,095** | 460 | Python is ~6.7x R (both tiny) |

- **Shiny** — Posit's flagship dual-language product — is the opposite: R downloads outpace Python by roughly 3x, and this holds over a 90-day window too (2.45M vs 729k).
- **dplyr and tidyverse** are R-only in this dataset (no tracked Python equivalent) and post some of the largest raw numbers of any package here (1.6M and 851k in 30 days) — a reminder that R's ecosystem isn't small, it's just not being compared apples-to-apples.

A couple of caveats given what this data can and can't tell you:
- **PyPI download counts are known to be inflated by bots/CI/mirrors** relative to CRAN's download logs, so raw PyPI vs. CRAN comparisons overstate Python's lead somewhat — this data source can't correct for that.

- The querychat/orbital numbers are small enough (hundreds to low thousands/month) that "Python is way more popular" there is really "Python is more popular among a tiny userbase" — worth not over-reading.

## How fast does the tidyverse team respond to issues?

**Scope of what's tracked:** this repo only collects GitHub data for 5 repos under the `tidyverse` GitHub org: **dplyr, ggplot2, ellmer, tidyverse (meta-package), and vitals**. Widely-used tidyverse packages like tidyr, purrr, stringr, readr, forcats, etc. aren't configured in `velocirepo.toml`, so I can't say anything about them.

**Method (proxy, not a built-in metric):** the raw data has `issue_open`, `comment`, and `issue_close` events per issue, but no explicit "responded"/"author association" field. I identified each repo's "team" as users who have ever merged ≥5 PRs (a decent proxy for maintainers — e.g. `romainfrancois`/`DavisVaughan`/`krlmlr`/`lionel-`/`hadley` for dplyr, `teunbrand`/`thomasp85`/`yutannihilation` for ggplot2). "Response time" = time from issue open to that repo's first comment from someone in that team set.

### First response time from a team member

| repo | issues (all-time) | % that got a team response | median time to first response | 75th pct |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ggplot2 | 4,459 | 86% | 7.8 hrs | 9.6 days |
| dplyr | 5,135 | 82% | 16.8 hrs | 11 days |
| ellmer | 487 | 72% | 15.0 hrs | 8 days |
| tidyverse (meta) | 264 | 69% | 11.8 hrs | 41 days |
| vitals | 169 | 42% | 39.7 hrs | 15.5 days |

**Last 12 months (since 2025-08-12)** — much faster, especially ggplot2 and dplyr, though sample sizes are small since issue volume on the older packages has dropped a lot:

| repo | issues opened | % responded | median response |
|---|---|---|---|
| ggplot2 | 195 | 85% | 2.3 hrs |
| dplyr | 65 | 57% | 9.1 hrs |
| ellmer | 176 | 71% | 14.6 hrs |
| vitals | 50 | 54% | 68.5 hrs |
| tidyverse (meta) | 2 | — | too few to say |

### Time to close an issue (median)

- vitals: 0.9 days
- tidyverse (meta): 4.2 days
- dplyr: 6.6 days
- ellmer: 9.1 days
- ggplot2: 12.4 days

### Takeaways
- On the actively-developed packages (ggplot2, ellmer), the team typically gives an initial response within a matter of hours, and most responded-to issues get a reply same-day.
- dplyr and the tidyverse meta-package are mature/low-traffic now, so response times are a bit slower and less consistent, though issue volume is also much lower than in their peak years (2015–2018).
- The 25th percentile response time across all repos is under 2 hours — i.e., a sizeable share of issues get an almost-immediate acknowledgment — while the tail (75th/90th percentile) stretches into days/weeks, often issues that need deeper investigation or get triaged later.
- vitals stands out as slower/less consistently responded-to, but it's a newer, smaller project (169 issues total, 11 merge-active contributors), so the "team" signal here is noisier.

**Caveats:** "team member" is inferred from merge activity, not actual GitHub team membership, which isn't in the collected data. "Response" counts any comment from that inferred team, not necessarily a substantive answer (could be a bot-like label/triage comment). If you want a stricter or different definition (e.g., only certain named maintainers, or excluding self-comments on issues they also opened), I can rerun with that definition.

I dug through the actual metrics files (the pre-built views in the DuckDB file reference absolute CI paths that don't resolve here, so I queried the underlying JSONL directly). Here's the honest picture:

**There is no "total audience" metric in this dataset.** Nothing in the collected sources (GitHub, PyPI, CRAN, Plausible, OpenVSX, YouTube, RSS) is stored as a unified reach/audience figure — I'd have to synthesize one, and the pieces that could plausibly represent "audience" have gaps that make a solid last-month comparison impossible:

1. **GitHub stars/followers — not tracked at all.** The GitHub event stream only records `issue_open/close`, `pr_open/merge`, `fork`, and `comment`. No `star` events, no follower counts anywhere in `data/metrics/github/*` (that source only has `total_reactions`).

   - End of June 2026: 47,500 subscribers (@PositPBC)
   - Latest reading in July 2026 (Jul 26, the last data point before month-end): 47,700 subscribers
   - **Growth: +200 subscribers (+0.4%)**

So "June" in this metric is really just 8 days (Jun 23–30) of partial-coverage data, while July has ~28 days of full coverage. Comparing those totals (~156K vs ~300K) would just be measuring the data-collection rollout, not real audience growth — I don't want to hand you a number that looks like a 2x jump in traffic when it's actually a tracking artifact.

   Note also: there's a separate `daily_visitors` metric per project, but that's broken out **per page** (e.g. dplyr has 100 rows per day, one per URL) — summing it would massively double-count the same visitors across pages, so it can't substitute here either.

4. **Downloads (PyPI/CRAN/OpenVSX)** measure usage, not audience/reach, so I didn't fold them in.

**Bottom line:** the only defensible "audience" growth figure I can give you for last month is YouTube: **+200 subscribers (+0.4%)**.
